DEX vs. CEX: Who Holds Your Money and Who Runs the Book
DEX vs. CEX: Who Holds Your Money and Who Runs the Book
You are the one in control now

On Binance or Bybit your balance is a number in their database. They hold the coins and they owe them to you. It works well, and it comes with password resets and support tickets precisely because somebody else is holding your money.
Onchain, you hold it. That is the whole point, and it is a genuine upgrade: no withdrawal limit set by someone else, no account freeze, no waiting on a ticket.
It does mean a few habits change. This module covers them, and none of them are difficult.

A wallet is a key. Whoever holds the key moves the money, and that is you. There is nothing to reset because there is nothing sitting on someone else's server to lose.
Two habits are worth building early.
Check your approvals. When you deposit to a DEX you sign a permission that lets the venue's contract move a token for you. Most wallets let you set a limit rather than leaving it open, and let you review or revoke it later. Two minutes at setup keeps you in charge of what each venue can touch.
Bring your own wallet. Some DEXs let you sign up with an email and create a wallet for you, which is convenient. If self custody is the reason you came, connect a wallet you made yourself and you keep the full benefit.
You can actually see where your order goes

On a CEX the matching engine is a black box. You trust it because the company is regulated and has a lot to lose. Onchain, you get to look inside.
Three setups you will come across:
Everything onchain. Every order, cancel and fill is written to the blockchain, so anyone can replay the book afterwards. Full transparency.
zk rollup. Matching runs off the main chain and the venue publishes cryptographic proof that it followed its own rules. You are trusting the maths rather than a promise.
Sequencer. One fast server confirms your order before it settles. This is what makes a good DEX feel as quick as a CEX.
Most venues pair the speed of a sequencer with one of the first two. Knowing which one you are on tells you how much of the venue you can verify for yourself.

Liquidations run off mark price, exactly as they do on a CEX, and mark price comes from an average of outside spot markets.
The difference onchain is that the method is usually public: which markets feed the average, and how often it refreshes. That is information a CEX never gives you, so use it.
Favour venues that publish both. And if you trade during quieter hours in your region, take a quick look at whether those source markets are deep at that time before setting a tight stop. It is a thirty second check that makes your stop more reliable.
Good venues have already planned for a bad day

Every platform has downtime. What is different onchain is that a well run venue publishes what happens next.
If the sequencer pauses, the site stops taking orders, but your position still exists and the blockchain keeps running. The better venues document an escape hatch: a way to withdraw straight from the blockchain without their help, audited so you can rely on it. Where that exists, an outage is an inconvenience rather than a worry.
Two more things worth a glance: whether the chain publishes its validator set, and which bridge your deposit crosses. Both are normal parts of trading onchain, and the venues that are open about them are the ones to prefer.
One habit that pays for itself: when you move funds, check the network twice. Onchain transfers settle exactly as instructed, so sending on the right chain first time is the single easiest way to keep the experience smooth.

Connect your own wallet. Set a limit on approvals. Pick venues that publish their price sources and their escape hatch. Do those three and you get the full upside of self custody with very little of the friction.

You hold the keys, so nothing gets frozen or reset. Connect a wallet you created yourself and set a limit on approvals, and you stay in charge of what each venue can touch.
Onchain, you can verify the venue instead of trusting it. Fully onchain books can be replayed by anyone, zk rollups publish proof they followed their own rules, and most venues publish the price sources behind your liquidation level.
Check the escape hatch before you deposit. A venue that documents an audited way to withdraw straight from the blockchain turns any outage into a minor inconvenience.

The Real Cost of a DEX Trade: Fees, Funding and Liquidation
The Real Cost of a DEX Trade: Fees, Funding and Liquidation
The good news is that you can measure all of it

Every venue advertises a maker and taker rate, and onchain some advertise zero. Fees are only part of the picture, and the useful part is that you can check every other part yourself.
Four things make up a round trip: the fee, the slippage, the funding, and the cost of moving money in and out. Add them up once per venue and the ranking you get is usually different from the one the fee table suggested, often in your favour.

A tight spread on a small order tells you little about a bigger one, so check the book at the size you actually trade, on both sides, at the hour you actually trade. You cross the spread twice, so quote the round trip rather than one side.
A worked example. A venue that is 0.02% cheaper per side looks like the obvious winner. If its book is thinner, a single awkward exit can hand back the whole saving. Depth is usually worth more than a basis point or two.
Then add deposits and withdrawals, spread across the number of trades you plan to make. Choose a venue that settles on a chain your exchange already withdraws to and that line almost disappears.
Funding is separate from fees, which keeps your cashback maths clean

Funding is the payment between longs and shorts that keeps the perp price near spot. It goes to other traders, not to the venue.
That is useful to know for two reasons. Your cashback applies to the fee line, so your cashback stays simple to calculate and nothing muddies it. And if you are choosing a venue for a multi hour hold, funding will matter more than the fee, so compare it first.
Intervals differ and both have an upside. Hourly funding charges more often but gives you more chances to exit before the next payment. On a four hourly schedule a quick trade may pay nothing at all. Most venues also cap how much a single interval can charge, which protects you during a squeeze.

Margin and liquidation prices work the way you already expect. The difference onchain is that you can see who absorbs a liquidation. It is usually a pool funded by other users who are earning yield for taking that risk.
Look for a venue that publishes three things: the size of that pool onchain, its auto deleveraging rules, and its incident history. Auto deleveraging is the mechanism that closes profitable positions on the winning side if the pool is ever used up, so it is worth understanding before you size up. A venue that publishes all three is telling you exactly how it behaves under stress, which is more than most CEXs will.
One practical tip: if topping up margin would mean a withdrawal plus a bridge hop, size the position so you never need to.

On a CEX, high volume usually means good liquidity. Onchain it can mean two things at once.
Many venues run points programmes that reward trading with a claim on a future token. That is real value to you, and it also lifts reported volume without depth necessarily following.
So treat volume as a signal rather than a measurement. Check depth at your size, then check where the programme sits in its cycle. A venue whose programme has finished and whose token is live is showing you volume that stands on its own. A venue still running one may be paying you to be early, which is worth knowing either way.

Build one number per venue: fees plus slippage at your size, both sides, plus the cost of getting in and out. Apply your cashback to the fee part. If you hold for hours, compare funding before fees. Prefer venues that publish their liquidation pool. It takes about ten minutes once, and it usually saves more than the cashback does.

The headline fee is one of four costs. Add fees, slippage at your size, funding, and the cost of moving money in and out. The best venue is often not the cheapest on paper.
Your cashback applies to the fee line. Funding goes to other traders rather than the venue, which keeps your cashback simple to work out and makes funding the first thing to compare on a longer hold.
Prefer venues that publish. A visible liquidation pool, clear auto deleveraging rules and a public incident history tell you how a venue behaves under pressure.

FX (Foreign Exchange): Trading one country's currency for another (e.g. swapping US Dollars for Euros). You are betting on which country's economy will perform better.
CFD (Contract for Difference): A type of trading where you do not own the actual currency. Instead, you are just betting on whether the price will go up or down. 
Key Takeaway: With CFDs, you are trading price movements, not buying real money.

Currencies are always traded in pairs (like EUR/USD). 
Base Currency (First): The currency you are buying.
Quote Currency (Second): The currency you are using to pay.
The Price: Tells you how much of the second currency it takes to buy one of the first. (If EUR/USD is 1.08, 1 Euro costs 1.08 US Dollars).
Leverage lets you trade with more money than you actually deposit by "borrowing" from the broker. While it can magnify your profits, it magnifies your losses just as fast.
A 1% move in the market becomes a 10% swing in your account  either up or down.
A 10% drop wipes out your entire $1,000
It’s the exact mirror of the $100 gain. The same small move, run 10x the other way, all the way to zero.

Every time you trade, you pay:
The Spread: The tiny difference between the buy and sell price. This is the broker's basic fee.
Swap / Overnight Fee: A fee charged if you keep your trade open until the next day.
Commission: A flat fee charged per trade by some brokers.
Slippage: When the market moves so fast, your trade gets filled at a worse price than expected.
These are the core terms you will encounter when reviewing broker offerings and trading conditions. Understanding them helps you compare products accurately.
The smallest standard price move in a currency pair. For most pairs, 1 pip = 0.0001 (4th decimal place). For JPY pairs, 1 pip = 0.01.
Standard lot = 100,000 units of base currency.  Mini lot = 10,000. Micro lot = 1,000. Determines the monetary value of each pip.
The deposit required to open and maintain a leveraged position. Expressed as a percentage of total position value.
Your account balance plus or minus the floating profit/loss of all open positions.
Straight Through Processing. Orders routed directly to liquidity providers without broker intervention. Typically lower conflict of interest.
Electronic Communications Network. Connects traders directly to interbank liquidity. Usually tighter spreads with commission per trade.
A portion of the spread or commission returned to a trader through an Introducing Broker (IB) or rebate partner like TetherMax.
An order to automatically close a position when it reaches a specified loss level. Essential for managing downside risk.

A trading platform designed mainly for forex trading. It is lightweight, easy to use, and popular with traders who want a straightforward charting and execution setup. Downloadable via desktop and mobile apps.
An advanced multi-market platform that supports forex plus stocks, futures, commodities, and other instruments, with charting tools, and order options. Downloadable via desktop and mobile apps.

A fee charged when you hold a position past the end of the trading day. It's calculated from the interest rate difference between the two currencies, so you can either pay it or earn it. It doesn't apply if you close your position the same day.
A warning that fires when your margin starts running low. It's a signal to either add funds or reduce your position.
If your margin keeps falling even after a margin call, the broker automatically closes your remaining positions at this level to keep your losses from growing further.
